transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-30 15:00 PT
Duration: 42m
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Roy (Redwood SE), Olivia Torres (Redwood CSM); Priya Kapoor (Velora Head of ML), Daniel Ortiz (Velora Infra), Lena Park (Velora PM), Marco Silva (Velora Eng)

Summary (auto): quick sync on tokens/sec/$ benchmarks from last week's run; discussed prefix cache gains, batching tradeoffs, and end-to-end latency targets; agreed follow-ups for microbenchmarks and cost sheet update.

00:00 Maya Chen: okay everyone good to go? hey hi, thanks for joining. i think we have 42 minutes on the calendar.
00:12 Priya Kapoor: yep thanks, we just want to go over the numbers from the pilot this week, and figure out next tuning steps. we've seen some savings but some variance at tail.
00:22 Samir Roy: quick context, last run was hosted inference on r-infer-4x (cc: internal shorthand), batch=2 by default, kv prefix cache enabled with a 30-minute TTL for repeated prompts. we measured tokens per second per dollar and also token cost per 1M tokens.
00:40 Daniel Ortiz: real quick: our success criteria for the POC is twofold — average latency < 400ms for 8k prompt flows and tokens/sec/$ >= 12 for our expected mix. 
00:54 Maya Chen: got it. note on the semantics: tokens/sec/$ here is token throughput divided by effective cost per second, we used the cost assumptions in the spreadsheet link I sent (see drive/velora/pilot-costs-v2.xlsx).
01:10 Lena Park: i wanted to call out that the mock traces we used skew shorter than production, so the caching benefits may be overestimated.
01:22 Samir Roy: agreed that matters. the good news: with prefix caching on, we saw an average 22% reduction in token compute for the repeated user flows in the trace set. the downside: 95th percentile latency increased slightly at high concurrency because of batching delays.
01:40 Marco Silva: can you quantify tokens/sec/$ please? numbers we got internally were around 9 tokens/sec/$ which is below target.
01:50 Samir Roy: from our aggregated run, with hosted config and batch=2, tokens/sec/$ = 11.6 avg, tokens/sec/$ at 95th percentile drops to about 8.3 due to quota tailing and queueing.
02:04 Priya Kapoor: that aligns with what we saw. when we pushed concurrent requests, some of the burst routing sent traffic to fallback model which had different quantization and cost — that added noise.
02:18 Maya Chen: yes, we had the smart routing policy set to fallback to a cheaper quantized variant when latency SLOs were at risk. That reduces cost per token but also changed quality in a few prompts in the eval set.
02:34 Daniel Ortiz: interesting tradeoff. are there knobs to keep tokens/sec/$ high but preserve P95 latency?
02:40 Samir Roy: lots of levers. quick hit: increase batch target to 4 or 8 — that improves throughput and lowers cost per token, but adds batching wait time; if typical per-request token length is high then batching helps more. Also caching TTL adjustments and prefix-only caching for certain routes can capture repeated prefixes without affecting fresh flows.
03:02 Priya Kapoor: what's the expected tokens/sec/$ improvement if we move batch=2 -> batch=8?
03:08 Samir Roy: ballpark from our microbench: for the model variant you're using, batch=2 -> batch=8 improved tokens/sec/$ by ~27% on average for long contexts ( >2k tokens ), but for short requests ( <200 tokens ) the gains shrink to ~8% and P95 latency can go up by 80-120ms because of batching startup.
03:32 Lena Park: that 80-120ms at p95 is non-trivial for our UX. our product team prefers p95 < 500ms.
03:40 Maya Chen: there's a middle ground: adaptive batching — keep batch target small during low QPS and enable larger packs when queue depth grows. That requires the runtime to switch policies and Samir can show settings.
03:52 Samir Roy: yeah we have an autoscaler that can vary batch windows based on queue latency signals. I can run a microbench that simulates your traffic shape (Priya's traces) and measure p50/p95/p99 for batch sizes 1/4/8 with autoscale on/off.
04:10 Priya Kapoor: please do. one more question on caching: you mentioned 22% compute reduction overall — is that tokens processed or cost savings?
04:18 Samir Roy: it's compute tokens reduced; cost savings translate to ~15% on net billing because some costs are fixed (reservation amortization in dedicated or baseline). In hosted, net billing showed ~18% lower token charge in the run.
04:30 Marco Silva: do you have numbers for token/sec/$ with cache on versus off?
04:35 Samir Roy: yes — cache off tokens/sec/$ = 9.4 avg; cache on = 11.6 avg in that run. but again, tail behavior was worse because cache hotspots cause microbursts that increase P95.
04:50 Priya Kapoor: microbursts how bad?
04:53 Samir Roy: in our traces the hotspot bursts increased p95 by ~90ms during the spike window. If traffic smoothing or request shaping is feasible on your side that reduces the P95 impact.
05:05 Daniel Ortiz: we can add a short client-side jitter and request shaping. not ideal but doable.
05:11 Maya Chen: other axis is model quantization. switching to int8-ish variant reduces cost per token by ~30% but may reduce quality on longer reasoning prompts — we flagged a few eval failures when we tried 4-bit earlier.
05:26 Priya Kapoor: quality is non-negotiable on our core flows. we prefer paying a premium over degraded outputs.
05:32 Maya Chen: understood. then favor batching/caching/route-policy over aggressive quantization for those routes.
05:40 Lena Park: what about dedicated vs hosted? if we move to dedicated reserved pools does that change tokens/sec/$ profile?
05:46 Samir Roy: yes, Dedicated gives a lower marginal cost when you run steady-state and you can tune kernels for better throughput. Our model shows dedicated reserved capacity drops effective cost per token by ~12-18% depending on commit. However, dedicated requires commit and has less instantaneous burst flexibility unless you enable burst credits.
06:06 Marco Silva: we were thinking dedicated for predictable cost, but worried about capacity planning if traffic spikes.
06:12 Maya Chen: you can set a hybrid policy: primary dedicated, overflow to hosted. Redwood's smart routing does that; cost model then becomes a weighted average. We can simulate your expected QPS with overflow rates and show tokens/sec/$ distribution.
06:28 Priya Kapoor: can you quantify the weighted tokens/sec/$ example? say 70% on dedicated at X and 30% on hosted at Y — what's combined?
06:36 Samir Roy: sure with numbers: dedicated tokens/sec/$ = 13.4, hosted tokens/sec/$ = 11.0; 70/30 blend = 12.8 tokens/sec/$. That's rough but we can produce a table in the sheet.
06:52 Daniel Ortiz: talk to me about autoscaler cooldowns and cost — we saw some oscillations that were charging more.
06:58 Samir Roy: most likely autoscaler was too aggressive on scale-up and slow to scale-down; that produces short-lived extra nodes with billing granularity effects. We recommend a scale-down cooldown of 5 minutes for your workload and a conservative upscale threshold. I can include tuned policies in the repo.
07:16 Priya Kapoor: please do. also we want to understand the 95th percentile latency goal — can Redwood guarantee that on hosted?
07:24 Maya Chen: we have SLO-backed offerings on Dedicated with SLA for uptime and latency tiers, but hosted offers best-effort low-latency; we publish reliable benchmarks but SLA-tiered latency guarantees are part of Dedicated/enterprise packages.
07:38 Priya Kapoor: ok. for now we'll stick with hosted for the POC.
07:42 Lena Park: a note on instrumentation: we need token-level cost breakdown in our telemetry to attribute costs by route and by feature flag. can Redwood expose per-route token/cost metrics?
07:52 Olivia Torres: yes, Redwood Console provides token-level and route-level breakdowns; we can also enable per-token tracing for a sampling rate. we'll include instructions for your telemetry team.
08:04 Marco Silva: great. will that include KV cache hit/miss metrics?
08:08 Olivia Torres: yes, cache hit/miss and ttl stats are exposed.
08:12 Priya Kapoor: perfect.
08:14 Maya Chen: quick callouts on the plan: Samir will run microbench with your traces and batch variations; I'll update the cost model and include dedicated/hybrid scenarios; Priya you will share three representative traces. Olivia will enable console telemetry and provide how-to.
08:32 Samir Roy: one more thing — we noticed in your test that fallback routing to the quantized variant happened at around 10% of requests during busy windows. If you want to avoid any cross-model quality shift we can disable automatic fallback and instead orchestrate canary routing with manual thresholds.
08:48 Priya Kapoor: we want manual control for now. automatic fallback caused confusion with the product team.
08:52 Maya Chen: noted. we'll flip that to manual canary for the remainder of POC.
08:56 Daniel Ortiz: operational question: what's the expected token accounting lag in console? we saw a 5-7 minute lag previously.
09:02 Olivia Torres: console shows near-real-time metrics within 1-2 minutes for most telemetry; billing-level reconciliation may be slightly delayed. the 5-7 minute lag you saw was from the demo region we used that day.
09:14 Priya Kapoor: okay. last aside — security/compliance: we reviewed SOC2 certs last week. any updates on data residency?
09:22 Maya Chen: for hosted we have region controls and can route to eu/west, us-west, ap-southeast in limited fashion; Private/VPC supports strict residency and on-prem if needed. For POC it's not blocking.
09:34 Priya Kapoor: good.
09:36 Maya Chen: recap of key tuning recommendations we discussed: 1) Samir to run batch microbench for 1/4/8 + autoscale options; 2) adjust prefix cache TTLs and only apply to identified high-reuse routes; 3) consider hybrid dedicated+hosted for steady-state with overflow; 4) quantization only for non-critical routes; 5) disable automatic fallback to quantized variant for now and use manual canaries.
09:58 Marco Silva: sounds actionable.
10:02 Priya Kapoor: thanks — we'll prioritize trace upload and expect the benchmarking artifacts.
10:07 Maya Chen: i'll send the updated spreadsheet and a short note on assumptions. Thanks everyone.
10:14 Meeting ended.
